Name: Automate for environmental impact
Guideline: Reduce a process's environmental footprint by automating specific activities, fully or partially (semi-automation), choosing which steps to automate based on where automation yields the greater ecological benefit compared to human execution.
Context: The catalog’s own example: a telecom company that switched from mailing paper invoices to emailing them, cutting cost and turnaround time while reducing paper waste in one change.

Name: Green Compensation
Guideline: When a process cannot be redesigned for sustainability due to internal or technical restrictions, trigger a parallel compensation activity (e.g. a certified environmental offset such as tree planting or renewable-energy investment) whenever the process runs, so its environmental impact is counterbalanced without changing the process itself.
Context: The catalog frames the trigger condition specifically: production waste from machinery that can’t be reduced without investing in new, expensive equipment is the typical case this pattern is meant for, instead of attempting a redesign that isn’t really feasible.

Name: Green Feature
Guideline: Identify prominent, easily communicable features of a product or its process that can be swapped for greener alternatives; even a marginal reduction in ecological footprint from a highly visible feature can substantially improve the organization's perceived environmental reputation.
Context: The catalog notes this pattern deliberately optimizes for visibility and communicability over raw impact size — a feature with a small ecological effect is still worth choosing if it’s the one customers will actually notice and associate with the brand.

Name: Green Variant
Guideline: Offer an alternative, lower-impact variant of a business process (different steps, resources, or partners) that achieves the same functional outcome as the original, letting customers choose between the conventional and green variant rather than replacing the existing process.
Context: The catalog’s example: a trading company offering eco-friendly, renewable-material packaging as a premium option alongside its standard plastic wrapping — customers choose, the original process isn’t replaced.

Name: Human Process Performance
Guideline: Where it reduces environmental impact, replace machine- or IT-driven activities that pollute or consume significant energy with human-performed activities, weighing the ecological gain against cost and efficiency trade-offs.
Context: The catalog’s worked example: a metal-parts manufacturer replacing energy-intensive laser-scanning inspection with manual quality checks by employees, lowering both environmental impact and cost.

Name: Shift Workload
Guideline: Shift computing or task execution to time windows when the power grid draws more heavily on renewable energy, using carbon-intensity forecast data to determine the appropriate execution window and lower the resulting CO2 emissions.
Context: This pattern needs carbon-intensity forecast data and scheduling tooling to work: it shifts execution to whichever window the forecast shows the grid drawing most heavily on renewables, rather than running on a fixed schedule regardless of the grid’s energy mix at that moment.
